title: Tort Law
topics: Psychiatric injury and pure economic loss

notes.h: Duty of care: from Donoghue to Robinson
notes.body:
Negligence requires (1) a duty of care, (2) breach, and (3) damage caused by the breach that is not too remote. Duty controls which harms, to which claimants, the law will compensate.

The modern approach
- Donoghue v Stevenson (1932): Lord Atkin's neighbour principle requires reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour.
- Caparo Industries v Dickman (1990): in a novel case the court considers whether harm was foreseeable, whether there was sufficient proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
- Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire (2018): Caparo is not a universal three-stage test. In established categories, such as physical injury caused by a positive act, a duty simply exists. Novel cases develop incrementally by analogy, with policy weighed in that process.

Acts and omissions
There is generally no duty to prevent harm caused by a third party or a natural event, or to confer a benefit (Smith v Littlewoods 1987; Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales 2015). The recognised exceptions are: assumption of responsibility; control over the third party (Home Office v Dorset Yacht 1970); the defendant creating or worsening the danger; and a special relationship with the claimant. Public bodies are treated like private persons: holding statutory powers that could have prevented harm does not by itself create a duty (Gorringe v Calderdale 2004; Poole BC v GN 2019; HXA v Surrey CC 2023). In Tindall v Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police (2024) officers who attended an icy road and then left had not made matters worse, so owed no duty to a motorist later killed there.

Police and hospitals
Police owe the ordinary duty for positive acts causing physical injury (Robinson), but not generally a duty to protect the public from criminals (Hill v CC West Yorkshire 1989; Michael). In Darnley v Croydon Health Services (2018) misleading waiting-time information from A&E reception staff fell within the established duty a hospital owes to patients who have booked in.

Worked illustration
A council driver carelessly reverses a lorry into a pedestrian: established category, duty exists, no need for a Caparo analysis. If the same council fails to remove a dangerous tree on a private neighbour's land, that is an omission, and a duty arises only if one of the exceptions applies.

Exam pitfalls
- Applying Caparo mechanically in every problem; after Robinson, first ask whether the facts fall within an established category.
- Describing Hill as a blanket police 'immunity'; it is an absence of duty in a particular type of case.
- Failing to identify whether the defendant acted or merely failed to act.

notes.h: Breach of duty: the standard of care
notes.body:
Breach asks whether the defendant fell below the objective standard of the reasonable person in their position (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks 1856).

Setting the standard
- Impersonal: a learner driver is judged against a reasonably competent driver (Nettleship v Weston 1971); a junior doctor against the standard of the post held (Wilsher v Essex AHA, CA 1986).
- Children: the standard of a reasonable child of the same age (Mullin v Richards 1998).
- Professionals: a doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion (Bolam v Friern HMC 1957), provided that opinion has a logical basis and survives scrutiny (Bolitho v City & Hackney HA 1998).
- Risk disclosure: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015) replaced Bolam for advice; doctors must take reasonable care to ensure the patient knows of material risks and reasonable alternatives. McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board (2023) held that whether an alternative is 'reasonable' is judged by the professional practice test.

Factors weighed together
- Probability of harm: Bolton v Stone (1951), where balls left the ground only rarely, so the risk was too small to require more.
- Seriousness of harm: Paris v Stepney BC (1951), where goggles were required for a worker already blind in one eye.
- Cost and practicality of precautions: Latimer v AEC (1953), where closing a flooded factory was not required.
- Social utility: Watt v Hertfordshire CC (1954), where an emergency justified a greater risk. Compensation Act 2006 s1 and the Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015 direct courts to consider deterring desirable activities, acting for the benefit of society, responsible approaches to safety, and heroic intervention.
- Knowledge at the time: Roe v Minister of Health (1954) judges conduct by the knowledge available then, not hindsight.

Proof
Breach is proved on the balance of probabilities. Where the thing was under the defendant's control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence, res ipsa loquitur supports an inference of negligence (Scott v London & St Katherine Docks 1865).

Worked illustration
A surgeon in her first week nicks an artery during a routine operation. She is judged as a reasonably competent surgeon in that post, not as a beginner. If a responsible and logically defensible body of surgeons would accept her technique, she is not in breach (Bolam; Bolitho).

Exam pitfalls
- Treating the Bolton/Paris/Latimer factors as a formula rather than a balancing exercise.
- Using Bolam for a failure to warn of risks: Montgomery governs disclosure.
- Lowering the standard for inexperience or nerves.

The claimant must show that the breach caused the damage in fact and in law, and that the damage is not too remote.

Factual causation
- 'But for': Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington HMC (1969). The patient would have died of arsenic poisoning even if properly examined, so the negligence did not cause death.
- Material contribution to harm: where harm is caused cumulatively, a more than negligible contribution suffices (Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw 1956; Bailey v MoD 2008; Williams v Bermuda Hospitals Board 2016).
- Material increase in risk: for mesothelioma, where science cannot show which exposure caused the disease, materially increasing the risk is enough (Fairchild v Glenhaven 2002, building on McGhee v NCB 1973). Barker v Corus (2006) made such liability proportionate, but Compensation Act 2006 s3 restored joint and several liability for mesothelioma. Sienkiewicz v Greif (2011) applied Fairchild to a single exposing defendant. Wilsher v Essex AHA (1988) refused to extend McGhee where several different agents might have caused the harm.
- Loss of a chance: no recovery in personal injury for losing a less than even chance of a better outcome (Hotson 1987; Gregg v Scott 2005), though lost commercial chances can be valued (Allied Maples v Simmons & Simmons 1995).
- Chester v Afshar (2004): a narrow exception where a failure to warn deprived the patient of an informed choice.

Successive causes
Baker v Willoughby (1970): a later tort does not reduce the first tortfeasor's liability for the original disability. Jobling v Associated Dairies (1982): a supervening natural illness is taken into account.

Intervening acts
- Third parties: a free, deliberate and informed act may break the chain, unless it was the very risk the defendant should have guarded against (Dorset Yacht). Knightley v Johns (1982): a police officer's serious error broke the chain.
- The claimant: highly unreasonable conduct may break it (McKew v Holland & Hannen & Cubitts 1969), but suicide caused by depression resulting from the tort did not (Corr v IBC Vehicles 2008).

Remoteness
The Wagon Mound (No 1) (1961): liability only for damage of a reasonably foreseeable kind. The exact way it happens need not be foreseen (Hughes v Lord Advocate 1963; Jolley v Sutton LBC 2000), though contrast Doughty v Turner (1964). Once the kind of injury is foreseeable, the defendant takes the victim as found (Smith v Leech Brain 1962).

Scope of duty
Khan v Meadows (2021) asks whether the harm falls within the risks the duty was meant to guard against, building on SAAMCO (1997).

Exam pitfalls
- Using Fairchild outside mesothelioma-type single-agent cases.
- Confusing the kind of damage (remoteness) with its extent (eggshell skull).
- Treating Chester as a general relaxation of causation.

notes.h: Psychiatric injury and pure economic loss
notes.body:
Both areas restrict recovery through special duty rules.

Psychiatric injury
The claimant must have a recognised psychiatric illness, not ordinary grief or distress (Hinz v Berry 1970).
- Primary victims are within the zone of physical danger or reasonably believe they are. Only physical injury need be foreseeable (Page v Smith 1996). Rescuers have no special status and must themselves be primary victims (White v CC South Yorkshire 1999).
- Secondary victims witness danger or injury to someone else. Alcock v CC South Yorkshire (1992) requires: a close tie of love and affection (presumed for parents, children and spouses, otherwise proved); proximity in time and space to the event or its immediate aftermath (McLoughlin v O'Brian 1983); perception with the claimant's own unaided senses, so not via television; and that psychiatric injury was foreseeable in a person of ordinary fortitude.
- Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust (2024): the secondary victim must witness an 'accident', meaning an external event causing or threatening injury. Relatives who witness a loved one's death or collapse from a disease negligently left undiagnosed cannot recover as secondary victims. The majority (6–1; lead judgment by Lord Leggatt and Lady Rose) also rejected any separate 'sudden shock' or 'horrifying event' requirement, and held that a doctor's duty to a patient does not extend to protecting relatives from witnessing the patient's illness or death. Lord Burrows dissented.

Pure economic loss
Financial loss not consequential on physical damage to the claimant's person or property is generally irrecoverable. In Spartan Steel v Martin (1973) the damaged melt and its profit were recoverable, but profits on further melts lost during the power cut were not. Murphy v Brentwood DC (1991), overruling Anns (1978), treats the cost of repairing a defective building as pure economic loss; homeowners may instead rely on the statutory duty in the Defective Premises Act 1972 s1.

The main exception is assumption of responsibility:
- Hedley Byrne v Heller (1964): a duty arises where the defendant voluntarily assumes responsibility and the claimant reasonably relies.
- Caparo (1990): auditors owed no duty to investors, because the accounts were not prepared to guide investment decisions.
- Henderson v Merrett (1995): the principle extends to the provision of services.
- White v Jones (1995): a disappointed beneficiary recovered against the solicitor who delayed drawing up a will.
- Steel v NRAM (2018): no duty where reliance by a non-client on a solicitor's statement was not reasonable.

Worked illustration
A surveyor values a modest house for a lender, knowing the buyer will rely on the report rather than commission their own. A duty is owed to the buyer (Smith v Eric S Bush 1990).

Exam pitfalls
- Treating every bystander as a primary victim.
- Overlooking the 'own unaided senses' and 'accident' requirements.
- Calling damage to the claimant's own property 'pure' economic loss.

Occupiers' liability
- An occupier is anyone with sufficient control; there may be several (Wheat v Lacon 1966).
- The Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 protects visitors (those with express or implied permission). Under s2(2) the common duty of care is to take reasonable care to see that the visitor is reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which they are permitted to be there.
- s2(3)(a): occupiers must expect children to be less careful than adults (Glasgow Corporation v Taylor 1922), though parents bear primary responsibility for very young children (Phipps v Rochester Corporation 1955).
- s2(3)(b): specialists can be expected to guard against risks ordinarily incident to their calling (Roles v Nathan 1963).
- s2(4)(a): a warning discharges the duty only if, in all the circumstances, it enables the visitor to be reasonably safe.
- s2(4)(b): no liability for an independent contractor's faulty work if the occupier reasonably entrusted the work, took reasonable steps to choose a competent contractor and, where appropriate, checked the work (Haseldine v Daw 1941).
- Business occupiers cannot exclude liability for negligent death or personal injury (UCTA 1977 s2(1); Consumer Rights Act 2015 s65).

The Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 governs non-visitors, chiefly trespassers. A duty arises under s1(3) only if the occupier is aware of the danger (or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists), knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the non-visitor is or may come near it, and the risk is one against which the occupier may reasonably be expected to offer some protection. Property damage is excluded (s1(8)). Tomlinson v Congleton BC (2003): there is no duty to protect adults against obvious risks they freely choose to run.

Product liability
Manufacturers owe a common law duty to consumers (Donoghue v Stevenson). The Consumer Protection Act 1987 Part I adds strict liability:
- s2: producers, own-branders and importers are liable; a supplier is liable if it fails to identify its own supplier or the producer when asked.
- s3: a product is defective if its safety is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect, considering marketing, warnings, expected uses and time of supply. A v National Blood Authority (2001) took a strict approach; Wilkes v DePuy (2016) preferred a holistic assessment including risks and benefits.
- s4: defences include the development risks defence in s4(1)(e), upheld in European Commission v UK (1997).
- s5: recoverable damage is death, personal injury, or loss of private property above £275, excluding the defective product itself.

Exam pitfalls
- Applying the 1957 Act to trespassers.
- Assuming a warning sign is automatically enough.
- Claiming the cost of the defective product itself under the CPA.

Private nuisance
Private nuisance is an unlawful interference with the use or enjoyment of land: encroachment, physical damage, or interference with amenity.
- Standing: only a claimant with a proprietary interest or exclusive possession can sue (Hunter v Canary Wharf 1997).
- Reasonableness: in Fearn v Tate Gallery (2023) the Supreme Court asked whether the defendant's use was a common and ordinary use of land; if not, whether it substantially interfered with the claimant's ordinary use. Intensive visual intrusion from a public viewing platform was actionable.
- Locality matters for amenity interference (Sturges v Bridgman 1879) but not for material physical damage (St Helen's Smelting v Tipping 1865).
- Malice can make otherwise reasonable conduct a nuisance (Christie v Davey 1893).
- Natural hazards: an occupier who knows of a hazard on their land must take reasonable steps measured by their resources (Sedleigh-Denfield v O'Callaghan 1940; Leakey v National Trust 1980).
- Coventry v Lawrence (2014): coming to the nuisance is generally no defence; planning permission does not authorise a nuisance, though it may bear on the character of the locality; courts have more freedom to award damages instead of an injunction than Shelfer (1895) suggested.

Rylands v Fletcher (1868)
Strict liability arises where the defendant brings onto land something likely to do mischief if it escapes, in the course of a non-natural use, and it escapes and causes damage. Transco v Stockport MBC (2003) treats the rule as a sub-species of nuisance:
- the thing must pose an exceptionally high risk if it escapes;
- the use must be extraordinary and unusual for its time and place;
- there must be an escape from land the defendant controls (Read v J Lyons 1947);
- damage of the relevant type must be foreseeable (Cambridge Water v Eastern Counties Leather 1994);
- personal injury is not recoverable, and the claimant needs an interest in land.
Defences include act of a stranger (Rickards v Lothian 1913), act of God, consent, statutory authority and the claimant's own default.

Public nuisance
Public nuisance materially affects the comfort of a class of the public (AG v PYA Quarries 1957). An individual can sue in tort only on proof of special damage beyond that suffered by the public generally. Manchester Ship Canal v United Utilities (2024) allowed nuisance claims over sewage discharges despite the Water Industry Act 1991.

Exam pitfalls
- Allowing a lodger or family member without a proprietary interest to sue.
- Claiming damages for personal injury under Rylands.
- Treating planning permission as a defence.

notes.h: Defamation and misuse of private information
notes.body:
Defamation
A statement is defamatory if it tends to lower the claimant in right-thinking people's estimation (Sim v Stretch 1936), and under the Defamation Act 2013 s1 it must cause or be likely to cause serious harm to reputation. Libel is permanent, including broadcasts and posts; slander is transient and usually needs special damage.

The claimant must prove:
- a defamatory meaning: the single natural and ordinary meaning to the ordinary reasonable reader, read in context (Stocker v Stocker 2019), or an innuendo meaning;
- the words refer to the claimant;
- they were published to at least one third party;
- serious harm: Lachaux v Independent Print (2019) held this is a matter of actual impact proved on the facts, though it can be inferred from the gravity of the words and the scale of publication. A body trading for profit must show serious financial loss (s1(2)).
Government bodies cannot sue (Derbyshire CC v Times Newspapers 1993). Limitation is one year.

Defences under the 2013 Act
- Truth (s2): the imputation is substantially true.
- Honest opinion (s3): the statement is opinion, indicates in general terms its basis, and an honest person could have held it on facts existing at the time.
- Public interest (s4): the statement was on a matter of public interest and the defendant reasonably believed publishing it was in the public interest (Serafin v Malkiewicz 2020). The common-law Reynolds defence was abolished by s4(6).
- Privilege: absolute (Parliament, court proceedings) and qualified (duty and interest; fair and accurate reports, s7).
- Website operators (s5) and innocent dissemination (Defamation Act 1996 s1); s10 bars suing secondary publishers unless suing the author, editor or publisher is not reasonably practicable.

Jury trial is no longer the default (s11).

Misuse of private information
There is no general privacy tort (Wainwright v Home Office 2003). Misuse of private information developed from breach of confidence under Articles 8 and 10 ECHR and is now a distinct tort (Vidal-Hall v Google 2015).
- Stage 1: did the claimant have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the information, considering all the circumstances (Campbell v MGN 2004; Murray v Express Newspapers 2008)? ZXC v Bloomberg (2022): as a general rule, a person under criminal investigation has a reasonable expectation of privacy in that fact before charge.
- Stage 2: balance Article 8 against Article 10 by intense focus on the specific rights claimed; neither has automatic priority.
Remedies include damages (Gulati v MGN 2015) and injunctions; for interim injunctions against publication HRA 1998 s12(3) requires likely success at trial.

Exam pitfalls
- Forgetting to address serious harm.
- Confusing truth with honest opinion.
- Citing Reynolds privilege as current law.

Vicarious liability
A defendant may be strictly liable for another person's tort. The test has two stages (Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society 2012; Trustees of the Barry Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses v BXB 2023):
1. Employment or a relationship akin to it. Cox v Ministry of Justice (2016): activities integral to the defendant's business, for its benefit, creating the risk. Barclays Bank v Various Claimants (2020): genuinely independent contractors do not count. In BXB an elder's relationship was akin to employment.
2. A close connection between that relationship and the tort, so that it is fair and just to hold the defendant liable (Lister v Hesley Hall 2001; Dubai Aluminium v Salaam 2002). Mohamud v WM Morrison (2016) imposed liability for a kiosk attendant's assault on a customer; WM Morrison v Various Claimants (2020) did not, because the employee leaked payroll data to pursue a personal vendetta. In BXB the rape was not closely connected to the elder's role.

Defences
- Contributory negligence: Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 s1 reduces damages to the extent the court thinks just and equitable, having regard to the claimant's share in responsibility. Froom v Butcher (1976): 25% for not wearing a seat belt where injury would have been avoided, 15% where it would have been less severe.
- Volenti non fit injuria: full knowledge of the risk and a voluntary agreement to accept it (ICI v Shatwell 1965; Morris v Murray 1991). It seldom succeeds against employers (Smith v Baker 1891) and is excluded for car passengers by Road Traffic Act 1988 s149.
- Illegality: Patel v Mirza (2016) adopted a policy-based approach; Henderson v Dorset Healthcare (2020) confirmed no recovery for loss flowing from the claimant's own sentence or deliberate crime (Gray v Thames Trains 2009).
- Limitation: six years for most torts (Limitation Act 1980 s2); three years for personal injury, running from accrual or the date of knowledge (ss11 and 14), with a discretion to disapply (s33).

Remedies
- Compensatory damages put the claimant where they would have been without the tort. Future personal injury losses use multipliers adjusted by the discount rate set under the Damages Act 1996; pain, suffering and loss of amenity follow the Judicial College Guidelines.
- Aggravated damages compensate injured feelings caused by the manner of the wrong.
- Exemplary damages: only for oppressive, arbitrary or unconstitutional action by government servants, conduct calculated to profit, or statutory authorisation (Rookes v Barnard 1964; Kuddus 2001).
- Injunctions are discretionary.

Exam pitfalls
- Forgetting to establish the primary tort before discussing vicarious liability.
- Running volenti where the claimant merely knew of a risk.
- Treating contributory negligence as a complete defence.

cards.f: What are the three elements a claimant must prove in negligence?
cards.b: A duty of care owed by the defendant, breach of that duty, and damage caused by the breach that is not too remote.

cards.f: State Lord Atkin's neighbour principle (Donoghue v Stevenson 1932).
cards.b: You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour: people so closely and directly affected that you ought to have them in contemplation.

cards.f: What three factors did Caparo v Dickman (1990) identify for novel duty situations?
cards.b: Reasonable foreseeability of harm, sufficient proximity between the parties, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.

cards.f: What did Robinson v CC West Yorkshire (2018) decide about the Caparo test?
cards.b: Caparo is not a universal three-stage test. Where a case falls within an established category, such as physical injury caused by a positive act, a duty exists without fresh policy analysis; novel cases develop incrementally by analogy.

cards.f: What is the general rule on liability for omissions, and which case states it?
cards.b: There is generally no duty to prevent harm caused by third parties or to confer a benefit (Smith v Littlewoods 1987; Michael v CC South Wales 2015).

cards.f: List the four main exceptions to the no-duty rule for omissions.
cards.b: Assumption of responsibility; control over the third party (Dorset Yacht 1970); creating or worsening the danger; and a special relationship with the claimant or the source of danger.

cards.f: Why did Hill v CC West Yorkshire (1989) deny a duty?
cards.b: The police owe no general duty to protect members of the public from crimes by third parties whose identity was unknown; there was insufficient proximity between the police and the victim.

cards.f: What was decided in Darnley v Croydon Health Services (2018)?
cards.b: Receptionists' misleading information about A&E waiting times breached the established duty a hospital owes to patients who have booked in; no new policy analysis was required.

cards.f: How did Poole BC v GN (2019) apply the omissions principle to public bodies?
cards.b: A council investigating a family's harassment by neighbours had not assumed responsibility to the children and owed no duty to protect them; statutory powers alone do not generate a common law duty.

cards.f: What did Tindall v CC Thames Valley Police (2024) decide?
cards.b: Officers who attended an icy road and left before it was made safe had not made matters worse, so owed no duty to a driver later killed there; failing to confer protection is not the same as causing harm.

cards.f: What is the standard of care in negligence?
cards.b: The objective standard of the reasonable person in the defendant's position, judged by what a reasonable person would or would not have done.

cards.f: Is a learner driver judged by a lower standard? Give the authority.
cards.b: No. Nettleship v Weston (1971) held a learner driver must meet the standard of a reasonably competent driver.

cards.f: State the Bolam test as qualified by Bolitho.
cards.b: A doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical opinion (Bolam 1957), provided that opinion is capable of withstanding logical analysis (Bolitho 1998).

cards.f: What did Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015) decide?
cards.b: Doctors must take reasonable care to ensure patients are aware of any material risks of a proposed treatment and of reasonable alternatives; disclosure is no longer governed by Bolam.

cards.f: How does Bolton v Stone (1951) differ from Paris v Stepney BC (1951)?
cards.b: Bolton concerns the low probability of harm (cricket balls rarely leaving the ground), so no breach. Paris concerns the seriousness of harm (a one-eyed worker), so extra precautions were required.

cards.f: What principle does Latimer v AEC (1953) illustrate?
cards.b: The cost and practicality of precautions: the employer acted reasonably in treating a flooded floor with sawdust and was not required to close the factory.

cards.f: What standard applies to a child defendant?
cards.b: The standard of a reasonable child of the same age (Mullin v Richards 1998).

cards.f: How does Roe v Minister of Health (1954) affect the assessment of breach?
cards.b: Conduct is judged by the knowledge available at the time, not with hindsight; a risk unknown to reasonable practitioners when the act occurred cannot found a breach.

cards.f: What is res ipsa loquitur and when does it help a claimant?
cards.b: An evidential principle allowing negligence to be inferred where the thing was under the defendant's control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence, absent an explanation (Scott v London & St Katherine Docks 1865).

cards.f: What did McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board (2023) add to Montgomery?
cards.b: Whether an alternative treatment is 'reasonable', and so must be disclosed, is decided by the professional practice test, applying Bolam.

cards.f: What is the 'but for' test? Give the leading case.
cards.b: Would the damage have occurred but for the defendant's breach? In Barnett v Chelsea & Kensington HMC (1969) the patient would have died anyway, so causation failed.

cards.f: When is 'material contribution to harm' sufficient for causation?
cards.b: Where the harm is caused cumulatively by tortious and non-tortious factors and the defendant's contribution was more than negligible (Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw 1956; Bailey v MoD 2008).

cards.f: What rule did Fairchild v Glenhaven (2002) establish?
cards.b: In mesothelioma cases where several employers exposed the claimant to asbestos and science cannot identify which exposure caused the disease, each defendant who materially increased the risk is liable.

cards.f: How did Parliament respond to Barker v Corus (2006)?
cards.b: Barker made Fairchild liability proportionate to each defendant's contribution to risk; the Compensation Act 2006 s3 restored joint and several liability for mesothelioma.

cards.f: Can a claimant recover for loss of a less than 50% chance of recovery in clinical negligence?
cards.b: No. Hotson v East Berkshire AHA (1987) and Gregg v Scott (2005) refused recovery for loss of a chance in personal injury.

cards.f: State the test for remoteness of damage in negligence.
cards.b: The defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable (The Wagon Mound (No 1) 1961).

cards.f: What is the eggshell skull rule?
cards.b: If injury of a foreseeable kind occurs, the defendant is liable for its full extent even if the claimant's pre-existing vulnerability made it more serious (Smith v Leech Brain 1962).

cards.f: Contrast Baker v Willoughby (1970) with Jobling v Associated Dairies (1982).
cards.b: In Baker a later tort did not reduce the first defendant's liability for continuing loss. In Jobling a later supervening illness was taken into account, reducing damages.

cards.f: When does a claimant's own conduct break the chain of causation?
cards.b: When it is wholly unreasonable, as in McKew v Holland & Hannen & Cubitts (1969). Suicide caused by depression resulting from the tort did not break the chain in Corr v IBC Vehicles (2008).

cards.f: What does Hughes v Lord Advocate (1963) show about remoteness?
cards.b: The precise manner of harm need not be foreseeable if the kind of harm (burns) was; boys burned by an unexpected explosion of a paraffin lamp recovered.

cards.f: What kind of harm must a psychiatric injury claimant prove?
cards.b: A recognised psychiatric illness, not mere grief, distress or anxiety (Hinz v Berry 1970).

cards.f: Who is a primary victim?
cards.b: Someone within the range of foreseeable physical injury, or who reasonably believes they are; only physical injury need be foreseeable (Page v Smith 1996).

cards.f: List the Alcock (1992) control mechanisms for secondary victims.
cards.b: A close tie of love and affection with the primary victim; proximity in time and space to the event or its immediate aftermath; perception with their own unaided senses; and foreseeability of psychiatric injury in a person of ordinary fortitude.

cards.f: What did White v CC South Yorkshire (1999) decide about rescuers and employees?
cards.b: Neither has special status: police officers who helped at Hillsborough could recover only if they were primary victims exposed to danger.

cards.f: What did Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust (2024) decide?
cards.b: A secondary victim must witness an accident, an external event causing or threatening injury. Relatives who saw a loved one's collapse or death from a negligently undiagnosed condition could not recover.

cards.f: What is pure economic loss?
cards.b: Financial loss that is not consequential on physical damage to the claimant's person or property, such as lost profits or the cost of repairing a defective product.

cards.f: Explain the outcome in Spartan Steel v Martin (1973).
cards.b: Damage to the metal in the furnace and the profit on that melt were recoverable as consequential loss, but profits lost on melts that could not be processed during the power cut were pure economic loss and irrecoverable.

cards.f: What is the basis of liability in Hedley Byrne v Heller (1964)?
cards.b: A voluntary assumption of responsibility by the defendant for a statement, combined with the claimant's reasonable reliance on it.

cards.f: Why did the auditors in Caparo (1990) owe no duty to investors?
cards.b: The statutory audit was to enable shareholders as a body to supervise management, not to guide individual investment decisions; the auditors did not know the claimant would rely on it for a takeover.

cards.f: Why was the cost of repairing a defective house irrecoverable in Murphy v Brentwood DC (1991)?
cards.b: It was pure economic loss, not damage to other property; the House of Lords overruled Anns (1978). The Defective Premises Act 1972 s1 offers a statutory alternative.

cards.f: What duty does the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 impose?
cards.b: The common duty of care: to take reasonable care to see that the visitor is reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which they are permitted to be there (s2(2)).

cards.f: Who is an 'occupier'? Give the authority.
cards.b: Anyone with a sufficient degree of control over the premises; there may be more than one occupier (Wheat v Lacon 1966).

cards.f: How does the 1957 Act treat children and specialists?
cards.b: Occupiers must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults (s2(3)(a); Glasgow Corporation v Taylor 1922) and may expect specialists to guard against risks of their calling (s2(3)(b); Roles v Nathan 1963).

cards.f: When does an occupier avoid liability for an independent contractor's work?
cards.b: Under s2(4)(b) if it was reasonable to entrust the work to a contractor, the occupier took reasonable steps to choose a competent one and, where appropriate, checked the work.

cards.f: State the three conditions for a duty under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 s1(3).
cards.b: The occupier is aware of the danger or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists; knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the non-visitor is or may come into its vicinity; and the risk is one against which it may reasonably be expected to offer some protection.

cards.f: What principle came from Tomlinson v Congleton BC (2003)?
cards.b: An occupier need not protect adults against obvious risks they freely choose to run, such as diving into shallow water; individual freedom and social value of activities weigh against a duty.

cards.f: Who can be liable under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 s2?
cards.b: Producers, those who hold themselves out as producers (own-branders), importers into the UK, and suppliers who fail to identify the producer or their own supplier when asked.

cards.f: What is the test of defect under CPA 1987 s3?
cards.b: Whether the safety of the product is not such as persons generally are entitled to expect, considering all the circumstances including marketing, instructions, warnings, expected uses and time of supply.

cards.f: What is the development risks defence?
cards.b: Under CPA s4(1)(e), the producer is not liable if the state of scientific and technical knowledge at the time did not allow the defect to be discovered by a producer of such products.

cards.f: What damage is not recoverable under the CPA 1987?
cards.b: Loss of or damage to the defective product itself, damage to business property, and property damage of £275 or less (s5).

cards.f: What are the three forms of private nuisance?
cards.b: Encroachment onto the claimant's land, physical damage to land, and unreasonable interference with the use and enjoyment of land (amenity).

cards.f: Who can sue in private nuisance? Give the authority.
cards.b: Only a person with a proprietary interest in the land or exclusive possession of it (Hunter v Canary Wharf 1997).

cards.f: Does the character of the locality matter in nuisance?
cards.b: Yes for interference with amenity (Sturges v Bridgman 1879), but not where there is material physical damage to property (St Helen's Smelting v Tipping 1865).

cards.f: How did Fearn v Tate Gallery (2023) frame the reasonableness inquiry?
cards.b: The court asks whether the defendant's use was a common and ordinary use of land and, if not, whether it substantially interfered with the ordinary use of the claimant's land; the claimant's sensitivity is not the focus.

cards.f: What did Coventry v Lawrence (2014) say about planning permission?
cards.b: Planning permission does not authorise a nuisance, although it may be relevant to the character of the locality and to the choice between an injunction and damages.

cards.f: Is 'coming to the nuisance' a defence?
cards.b: Generally no (Sturges v Bridgman; Coventry v Lawrence), although a change in the claimant's use after the defendant's activity began may be relevant.

cards.f: What are the requirements for liability under Rylands v Fletcher after Transco (2003)?
cards.b: The defendant brought onto land something posing an exceptionally high risk if it escapes, in the course of an extraordinary and unusual use; it escaped from land under the defendant's control; and it caused foreseeable damage of the relevant type to the claimant's land.

cards.f: What did Cambridge Water v Eastern Counties Leather (1994) add to Rylands?
cards.b: Foreseeability of damage of the relevant type is required, so Rylands is not wholly strict.

cards.f: When can an individual sue in public nuisance?
cards.b: Only if they suffered special damage beyond that suffered by the public generally.

cards.f: What duty did Leakey v National Trust (1980) recognise?
cards.b: An occupier who knows or ought to know of a natural hazard on its land threatening a neighbour must take reasonable steps, measured partly by its resources, to prevent damage.

cards.f: What is the test for whether a statement is defamatory at common law?
cards.b: Whether it tends to lower the claimant in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally (Sim v Stretch 1936).

cards.f: Distinguish libel from slander.
cards.b: Libel is defamation in permanent form, including broadcasts and online publications, and is actionable without proof of special damage. Slander is transient and generally requires proof of special damage.

cards.f: What does s1 of the Defamation Act 2013 require?
cards.b: The statement must have caused or be likely to cause serious harm to the claimant's reputation; for a body trading for profit, harm must be serious financial loss.

cards.f: How did Lachaux v Independent Print (2019) interpret serious harm?
cards.b: It is a factual question about the actual impact of the statement, proved by evidence or inferred from the gravity of the words and scale of publication, not merely the inherent tendency of the words.

cards.f: State the elements of the honest opinion defence (2013 Act s3).
cards.b: The statement was one of opinion; it indicated in general or specific terms the basis of the opinion; and an honest person could have held the opinion on the basis of any fact existing when it was published.

cards.f: State the public interest defence (2013 Act s4).
cards.b: The defendant must show the statement was on a matter of public interest and that it reasonably believed publishing it was in the public interest; it replaced Reynolds privilege.

cards.f: Can a local authority sue in defamation?
cards.b: No. Derbyshire CC v Times Newspapers (1993) held that governmental bodies cannot sue, as it would chill free speech on public affairs.

cards.f: State the two-stage test for misuse of private information.
cards.b: First, did the claimant have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the information? Second, does the Article 8 interest outweigh the publisher's Article 10 right to freedom of expression on the facts?

cards.f: What did ZXC v Bloomberg (2022) decide?
cards.b: As a legitimate starting point, a person under criminal investigation has a reasonable expectation of privacy in that information before being charged.

cards.f: What does HRA 1998 s12(3) require for an interim injunction restraining publication?
cards.b: The applicant must show they are likely to establish at trial that publication should not be allowed; usually meaning more likely than not (Cream Holdings v Banerjee 2004).

cards.f: What are the two stages of vicarious liability?
cards.b: A relationship of employment or one akin to employment between defendant and tortfeasor, and a close connection between that relationship and the tort making it fair and just to impose liability.

cards.f: What did Barclays Bank v Various Claimants (2020) decide?
cards.b: A bank was not vicariously liable for a self-employed doctor who carried on his own independent business; the relationship was not akin to employment.

cards.f: Contrast Mohamud v Morrison (2016) with Morrison v Various Claimants (2020).
cards.b: In Mohamud an assault by a kiosk attendant on a customer was closely connected to his job. In the 2020 case an employee leaking payroll data to harm his employer was on a personal frolic, so no liability.

cards.f: What did Trustees of the Barry Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses v BXB (2023) decide?
cards.b: An elder's relationship with the organisation was akin to employment, but the rape he committed was not closely connected to his role, so there was no vicarious liability.

cards.f: What is the effect of contributory negligence?
cards.b: Damages are reduced to the extent the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in responsibility (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 s1); it is not a complete defence.

cards.f: What reductions did Froom v Butcher (1976) suggest for failure to wear a seat belt?
cards.b: 25% where wearing one would have prevented the injury entirely, 15% where it would have made the injury less severe, and none where it would have made no difference.

cards.f: What must be shown for volenti non fit injuria?
cards.b: That the claimant, with full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk, freely and voluntarily agreed to accept it.

cards.f: What was decided in Henderson v Dorset Healthcare (2020)?
cards.b: A claimant who killed her mother while ill could not recover for losses flowing from her conviction and sentence; Gray v Thames Trains was consistent with Patel v Mirza.

cards.f: What is the limitation period for personal injury claims in negligence?
cards.b: Three years from the date of the cause of action or the date of knowledge if later (Limitation Act 1980 ss11 and 14), subject to the court's discretion under s33.

cards.f: In what categories are exemplary damages available?
cards.b: Oppressive, arbitrary or unconstitutional action by servants of the government; conduct calculated to make a profit exceeding compensation; and where statute authorises them (Rookes v Barnard 1964).

questions.q: Which case established the 'neighbour principle'?
questions.why: Lord Atkin set out the neighbour principle in Donoghue v Stevenson; Caparo and Robinson concern later approaches to novel duties.

questions.q: A learner driver hits a pedestrian while driving carefully for a beginner. What standard of care applies?
options: That of a reasonable learner driver
That of the defendant doing their honest best
That of a reasonably competent and experienced driver
No duty is owed while supervised
questions.why: Nettleship v Weston (1971) applies the standard of a reasonably competent driver regardless of inexperience.

questions.q: In which situation does the Fairchild exception to 'but for' causation apply?
options: Any industrial disease with several possible causes
Mesothelioma where several employers exposed the claimant to asbestos
Clinical negligence where a chance of recovery was lost
Cases where two different toxic agents might have caused the injury
questions.why: Fairchild applies where a single agent (asbestos) causes an indivisible disease and science cannot identify the responsible exposure; Wilsher refused an extension to multiple agents.

questions.q: Following Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust (2024), which claimant is most likely to fail as a secondary victim?
options: A mother who sees her son crushed by a negligently driven lorry
A husband who arrives at the scene of a rail crash minutes after it happens and sees his injured wife
A daughter who witnesses her father collapse and die at home from a heart condition a doctor negligently failed to diagnose months earlier
A father who sees his daughter struck by a falling crane
questions.why: Paul requires the claimant to witness an accident, an external event; a death from an undiagnosed medical condition is not one.

questions.q: Under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, which type of loss can a trespasser not recover?
options: Psychiatric illness caused by an injury
questions.why: Section 1(8) excludes liability for loss of or damage to property under the 1984 Act.

questions.q: Which claimant cannot sue in private nuisance after Hunter v Canary Wharf (1997)?
options: A freehold owner occupying the house
A freeholder whose reversion is permanently damaged
The adult child of the owner, living at home with no interest in the property
questions.why: Standing in private nuisance requires a proprietary interest or exclusive possession; a mere licensee family member has none.

questions.q: Which defence under the Defamation Act 2013 replaced Reynolds privilege?
options: Publication on a matter of public interest (s4)
questions.why: Section 4 created the public interest defence, and s4(6) abolished the common law Reynolds defence.

questions.q: In Barclays Bank v Various Claimants (2020), why was the bank not vicariously liable for the doctor's assaults?
options: The assaults were not closely connected to the examinations
The doctor was an independent contractor carrying on his own business
questions.why: The Supreme Court held that the first stage failed: the doctor's relationship with the bank was not akin to employment.

questions.q: A claimant's leg is negligently injured by D1. Before trial he develops an unrelated illness that would have disabled him anyway. Which case suggests the illness reduces D1's liability?
questions.why: In Jobling the House of Lords took a supervening natural illness into account; Baker concerned a supervening tort.

questions.q: Which statement about Rylands v Fletcher is correct after Transco v Stockport MBC (2003)?
options: No escape from the defendant's land is required
The use must be extraordinary and unusual and the thing must pose an exceptionally high risk
questions.why: Transco required an exceptionally high risk and extraordinary use; Cambridge Water requires foreseeability, Read v Lyons an escape, and Transco excludes personal injury.

questions.q: Explain how Robinson v CC West Yorkshire (2018) changed the approach to establishing a duty of care.
markScheme: Caparo is not a universal three-stage test
In established categories a duty follows from precedent without fresh policy analysis
Physical injury caused by a positive act is an established category, so police owed a duty
Novel cases are decided incrementally by analogy with existing law
questions.modelAnswer: Robinson held that Caparo had been misread as a universal test requiring foreseeability, proximity and fairness in every case. Where the facts fall within an established category, such as carelessly causing physical injury by a positive act, a duty simply exists. The officers who knocked over Mrs Robinson while arresting a suspect therefore owed her a duty, as anyone would. Only in genuinely novel situations does the court reason incrementally from decided cases, weighing policy as part of that process.

questions.q: Explain the difference between Bolam and Montgomery in clinical negligence.
markScheme: Bolam: not negligent if supported by a responsible body of medical opinion
Bolitho: that opinion must withstand logical analysis
Montgomery: disclosure of risks is not governed by Bolam
Duty to take reasonable care to ensure patient is aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives
Materiality judged from a reasonable person in the patient's position or what the doctor knows this patient would consider significant
questions.modelAnswer: Bolam (1957) governs diagnosis and treatment: a doctor is not negligent if acting in accordance with a practice accepted by a responsible body of medical opinion, provided after Bolitho (1998) that it has a logical basis. Montgomery (2015) removed risk disclosure from Bolam. A doctor must take reasonable care to ensure the patient knows of material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would likely attach significance to it, or the doctor knows or should know this patient would.

questions.q: What is the test for remoteness of damage in negligence and how is it qualified by the eggshell skull rule?
markScheme: Damage must be of a reasonably foreseeable kind (The Wagon Mound (No 1))
Precise manner and extent need not be foreseen (Hughes v Lord Advocate)
Defendant takes the victim as found: liable for full extent once kind is foreseeable (Smith v Leech Brain)
questions.modelAnswer: Under The Wagon Mound (No 1) (1961) a defendant is liable only for damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable. The precise way it occurs and its extent need not be foreseen (Hughes v Lord Advocate 1963). The eggshell skull rule means that once some injury of a foreseeable kind occurs, the defendant is liable for its full consequences even if a pre-existing vulnerability made them far worse, as in Smith v Leech Brain (1962), where a burn triggered fatal cancer.

questions.q: Why is pure economic loss generally irrecoverable in negligence, and what is the main exception?
markScheme: Fear of indeterminate liability to an indeterminate class
Contract is usually the better allocator of economic risk
Spartan Steel or Murphy as illustration
Exception: assumption of responsibility plus reasonable reliance (Hedley Byrne; Henderson v Merrett)
questions.modelAnswer: Courts fear liability in an indeterminate amount to an indeterminate class, and consider that economic risks are usually best allocated by contract. In Spartan Steel (1973) profits lost during a power cut were irrecoverable, and Murphy v Brentwood (1991) treated the cost of repairing a defective building as pure economic loss. The main exception is Hedley Byrne v Heller (1964): where the defendant voluntarily assumes responsibility for a statement or service and the claimant reasonably relies on it, a duty arises (Henderson v Merrett 1995).

questions.q: State when a warning sign discharges an occupier's duty under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957.
markScheme: s2(4)(a): warning must enable the visitor to be reasonably safe in all the circumstances
Mere notice is not automatically enough
Relevant factors: clarity, visibility, nature of danger, whether alternatives were available
No warning needed for obvious risks (e.g. Darby v National Trust 2001)
questions.modelAnswer: Under s2(4)(a) a warning discharges the duty only if, in all the circumstances, it was enough to enable the visitor to be reasonably safe. A sign must be clear, visible and specific enough to identify the danger, and a visitor who cannot avoid the danger, for example because the only route passes it, may still need physical protection. Where a risk is obvious, no warning may be needed at all, as in Darby v National Trust (2001), concerning the obvious risks of swimming in a pond.

questions.q: Outline the relevance of malice, locality and planning permission in private nuisance.
markScheme: Malice can make otherwise reasonable conduct unreasonable (Christie v Davey)
Locality relevant to amenity interference (Sturges v Bridgman)
Not relevant to physical damage (St Helen's Smelting v Tipping)
Planning permission is not a defence (Coventry v Lawrence)
But it may affect character of locality or the remedy
questions.modelAnswer: Nuisance turns on reasonable give and take between neighbours. Malice can turn otherwise reasonable conduct into a nuisance, as with deliberate noise in Christie v Davey (1893). The character of the locality matters for amenity interference, so conduct acceptable in an industrial area may be a nuisance in a quiet residential one (Sturges v Bridgman 1879). It is irrelevant where there is material physical damage (St Helen's Smelting v Tipping 1865). Planning permission does not authorise a nuisance, but it may affect the character of the locality or whether damages are awarded instead of an injunction (Coventry v Lawrence 2014).

questions.q: Explain the serious harm requirement in s1 of the Defamation Act 2013.
markScheme: Statement must cause or be likely to cause serious harm to reputation
Lachaux: question of fact about actual impact
Can be proved by evidence or inferred from gravity and extent of publication
Not just the inherent tendency of the words
For profit-making bodies: serious financial loss (s1(2))
Raised the threshold above the common law Thornton seriousness test
questions.modelAnswer: Section 1 adds a statutory requirement that the statement has caused or is likely to cause serious harm to reputation. In Lachaux v Independent Print (2019) the Supreme Court held this depends on the actual impact of the words, a question of fact, not merely their inherent tendency. Harm may be proved by evidence or inferred from the gravity of the imputation, the size and nature of the audience and other circumstances. A body trading for profit must show serious financial loss (s1(2)). The provision raised the bar above the common law threshold of seriousness (Thornton v Telegraph Media 2010).

questions.q: What must a defendant show to establish volenti non fit injuria?
markScheme: Claimant had full knowledge of the nature and extent of the risk
Claimant freely and voluntarily agreed to accept that risk (express or implied)
Mere knowledge is insufficient; rarely succeeds for employees; barred for passengers by RTA 1988 s149
questions.modelAnswer: The defendant must show that the claimant knew the nature and extent of the risk and freely and voluntarily agreed, expressly or impliedly, to accept the legal risk of harm. Knowing of a risk is not enough. The defence rarely succeeds against employers because employees act under economic pressure (Smith v Baker 1891), and Road Traffic Act 1988 s149 prevents drivers relying on it against passengers. It succeeded in Morris v Murray (1991), where the claimant flew with an obviously very drunk pilot.

questions.q: Explain the general rule that there is no liability for omissions and give two exceptions with authority.
markScheme: No duty to prevent harm by third parties or confer a benefit (Smith v Littlewoods; Michael)
Rationale: autonomy, 'why pick on me', burden of positive duties
Exception 1, e.g. control over third party: Dorset Yacht
Exception 2, e.g. assumption of responsibility or creating the danger, with authority
questions.modelAnswer: The common law generally imposes no duty to protect others from harm caused by third parties or natural events, or to confer a benefit (Smith v Littlewoods 1987; Michael v CC South Wales 2015). Positive duties restrict liberty and raise the question of why one person should be singled out. One exception is control: in Home Office v Dorset Yacht (1970) officers who negligently let borstal boys escape owed a duty to nearby boat owners. Another is assumption of responsibility, for example an employer undertaking to look after employees.

questions.q: Explain the test for a 'defect' under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 s3 and the debate about how it is applied.
markScheme: Safety not such as persons generally are entitled to expect
Circumstances: marketing, get-up, instructions, warnings, expected use, time of supply
A v National Blood Authority: strict approach, avoidability and risk-benefit irrelevant to the standard
Wilkes v DePuy: holistic approach, risk-benefit and regulatory compliance may be considered
Defect assessed by the general public's legitimate expectation, not the claimant's
questions.modelAnswer: A product is defective if its safety is not what persons generally are entitled to expect, taking account of all the circumstances, including marketing, instructions, warnings, reasonably expected uses and the time of supply. In A v National Blood Authority (2001) Burton J held that avoidability was irrelevant: if the public was entitled to expect blood free of hepatitis C, a non-standard product was defective. In Wilkes v DePuy (2016) Hickinbottom J preferred a flexible, holistic approach in which risk-benefit factors, regulatory approval and the cost of safety may inform legitimate expectations. Expectations are those of the public generally, not the individual claimant.

questions.q: Marta, a council-employed park warden, sees teenagers lighting a bonfire next to a wooden pavilion at closing time. She tells them to stop but leaves without calling the fire service or locking the gates. The fire spreads, injuring Leo, a jogger passing on a public path, and destroying Ivan's adjoining shed. Separately, a council officer, Owen, while chasing a suspected vandal through the park, knocks over Priya, an elderly visitor, breaking her hip. Advise Leo, Ivan and Priya on whether the council owes them a duty of care.
markScheme: Identify vicarious liability of council for employees' torts
Robinson: established category for Owen's positive act causing physical injury; duty owed to Priya
No need for Caparo analysis in established categories
Marta's conduct is an omission: no general duty to prevent harm by third parties (Smith v Littlewoods; Michael)
Consider exceptions: control (Dorset Yacht), assumption of responsibility, creating the danger
Did Marta make things worse? Compare Tindall: no duty where defendant does not worsen position
Public body status: statutory powers alone do not create duty (Gorringe; Poole v GN)
Occupier angle: council as occupier with knowledge of hazard (Sedleigh-Denfield) for Ivan's shed in nuisance
Reasoned conclusion on each claimant
questions.modelAnswer:
The council is vicariously liable for its employees' torts committed in the course of employment, so the question is whether Marta and Owen personally owed duties.

Priya: Owen's chase is a positive act that carelessly caused physical injury. Following Robinson v CC West Yorkshire (2018), this is an established category: no special policy analysis is required, and a public official is treated like any private person. A duty is owed. Whether Owen breached it depends on the reasonableness of chasing someone through a park with elderly visitors nearby, but on these facts breach looks arguable.

Leo: The harm was caused by the teenagers, third parties, and Marta failed to prevent it. The general rule is that there is no duty to prevent harm caused by third parties (Smith v Littlewoods 1987; Michael 2015). Leo must bring himself within an exception. There was no control over the teenagers as in Dorset Yacht, since they were not in the council's custody. Marta did not create the danger; in Tindall (2024) officers who attended a hazard and left without making it worse owed no duty. Leo may argue that the council, as occupier, had assumed responsibility for park safety, but Poole BC v GN (2019) and Gorringe (2004) indicate statutory functions alone do not generate a duty. Leo's claim in negligence is weak. The occupiers' liability Acts are unlikely to help, since the danger came from third parties' activity rather than the state of the premises, and users of public rights of way are not visitors (McGeown v Northern Ireland Housing Executive 1995).

Ivan: His best route is private nuisance. An occupier who knows of a hazard created by trespassers on its land and fails to take reasonable steps to abate it may be liable to neighbours (Sedleigh-Denfield v O'Callaghan 1940; Smith v Littlewoods recognised this exception where the occupier knows of a fire risk created by third parties). Marta's actual knowledge and the ease of calling the fire service suggest liability.

Conclusion: Priya very likely has a claim; Ivan has a good claim in nuisance; Leo's negligence claim is likely to fail.

questions.q: Dr Hale, a newly qualified GP, prescribes a medicine to Sam, who has a rare allergy noted on his file. Dr Hale did not read the file because the surgery was busy; most GPs would check. Sam suffers a severe reaction. In a separate consultation Dr Hale recommends knee surgery to Tia without mentioning a 2% risk of nerve damage or the option of physiotherapy. Tia, a professional dancer, suffers nerve damage. A group of orthopaedic surgeons say they would not mention a 2% risk. Advise Sam and Tia on breach of duty.
markScheme: Objective standard; inexperience irrelevant (Nettleship; Wilsher CA)
Bolam test for diagnosis and treatment
Bolitho: opinion must withstand logical analysis
Failing to read file almost certainly below standard; busyness not an excuse
Montgomery governs risk disclosure for Tia
Materiality: reasonable person in patient's position or this patient's known concerns; dancer's career
Reasonable alternatives (physiotherapy) must be disclosed; McCulloch on what is reasonable
Surgeons' contrary practice irrelevant to disclosure after Montgomery
Note causation as separate issue (would Tia have declined; Chester v Afshar)
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Breach is judged objectively against the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner in the defendant's post. Inexperience does not lower the standard (Nettleship v Weston 1971; Wilsher v Essex AHA, CA 1986), so Dr Hale is judged as a reasonably competent GP.

Sam: Treatment decisions are governed by Bolam (1957): Dr Hale is not negligent if a responsible body of medical opinion would support prescribing without checking the patient's record. The facts state most GPs would check. Even if some GPs did not, Bolitho (1998) requires that opinion to withstand logical analysis; a practice of ignoring recorded allergies would be indefensible given the serious and easily avoided risk. Busyness does not excuse failing to take a basic, low-cost precaution, especially where the potential harm is severe (compare Paris v Stepney 1951 on gravity of harm). Breach is very likely.

Tia: Risk disclosure is governed by Montgomery v Lanarkshire (2015), not Bolam. Dr Hale had to take reasonable care to ensure Tia was aware of material risks and reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in her position would attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows or should know this patient would. A 2% risk of nerve damage is plainly significant to a professional dancer whose livelihood depends on her knees. The surgeons' practice of not mentioning it is irrelevant to disclosure after Montgomery. Physiotherapy appears to be a reasonable alternative; under McCulloch v Forth Valley (2023), whether it is reasonable is judged by professional opinion, and if responsible doctors regard it as reasonable it had to be mentioned. Breach is likely.

Causation remains separate: Tia must show she would not have had the surgery, or would have deferred it, if properly informed. If she would have delayed, Chester v Afshar (2004) may assist.

Conclusion: both Sam and Tia are likely to establish breach.

questions.q: Harry worked for three employers, A Ltd, B Ltd and C Ltd, each of which negligently exposed him to asbestos. He develops mesothelioma; C Ltd is insolvent and uninsured. Meanwhile Grace is negligently struck by Dan's van, fracturing her pelvis. While she is in hospital, a nurse gives her a drug which, because of a rare pre-existing condition, causes a stroke. A year later Grace develops an unrelated degenerative spine disease that would have ended her career anyway. Advise Harry and Grace on causation and remoteness.
markScheme: But for test fails for Harry because the responsible exposure cannot be identified
Fairchild: material increase in risk suffices for mesothelioma
Barker v Corus apportionment reversed by Compensation Act 2006 s3: joint and several liability
Harry can recover full damages from A or B; contribution between defendants; insolvency risk on solvent defendants
Grace: but for test satisfied for pelvis injury
Nurse's act as possible novus actus: medical negligence rarely breaks chain unless grossly unreasonable (Knightley v Johns contrast)
Eggshell skull: stroke from pre-existing condition (Smith v Leech Brain), if nurse's act not intervening
Remoteness: kind of harm foreseeable (Wagon Mound; Hughes)
Supervening illness: Jobling reduces damages for loss of earnings after onset
Contrast Baker v Willoughby
Reasoned conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
Harry: On the 'but for' test Harry cannot show which employer's exposure caused his mesothelioma. Fairchild v Glenhaven (2002) created an exception: where several defendants negligently exposed a claimant to asbestos, each is liable if it materially increased the risk. Barker v Corus (2006) made that liability proportionate to each defendant's share of exposure, which would leave Harry bearing C Ltd's share. However, the Compensation Act 2006 s3 provides that in mesothelioma cases defendants are jointly and severally liable. Harry can recover his full damages from A Ltd or B Ltd, who may seek contribution from each other under the Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978; C Ltd's insolvency is their risk, not his.

Grace: But for Dan's negligence she would not have fractured her pelvis or been in hospital, so factual causation is satisfied for the initial injury.

The nurse's act: an intervening act breaks the chain only if it is sufficiently independent and unreasonable. Negligent medical treatment of injuries caused by a tort is generally foreseeable and will not normally break the chain unless it is grossly negligent or wholly unexpected, by analogy with the reasoning in Knightley v Johns (1982). If the nurse was not negligent, the stroke resulted from Grace's pre-existing vulnerability. Under the eggshell skull rule (Smith v Leech Brain 1962), once injury of a foreseeable kind is suffered, Dan takes his victim as he finds her, and the precise mechanism need not be foreseen (Hughes v Lord Advocate 1963). If she was negligent, the hospital may also be liable, but the chain breaks only if her negligence was egregious.

The spine disease: a supervening natural illness is taken into account because it is one of the vicissitudes of life (Jobling v Associated Dairies 1982). Dan's liability for loss of earnings ends when the disease would have ended her career. This differs from Baker v Willoughby (1970), which concerned a second tort.

Conclusion: Harry recovers in full against A Ltd or B Ltd; Grace recovers for the fracture and probably the stroke, with future loss of earnings capped by Jobling.

questions.q: At a music festival a stage collapses because of the organiser's negligence, crushing Ben. His wife Cara, standing 20 metres away, sees it happen and develops PTSD. Ben's brother Dev watches a live stream at home and develops depression. Eli, a steward helping to lift debris, is never in danger but develops PTSD. Fay, Ben's mother, arrives at the hospital three hours later and sees Ben before he is cleaned up, then develops a severe anxiety disorder. Advise each claimant.
markScheme: Need recognised psychiatric illness (all have one)
Distinguish primary and secondary victims (Page v Smith; White)
Cara: secondary victim satisfying Alcock: presumed close tie, proximity, own senses
Dev: brother must prove close tie; live stream fails 'own unaided senses' (Alcock on TV)
Eli: rescuer has no special status (White); not primary victim unless in danger or reasonably believing so
Fay: presumed tie; immediate aftermath question: McLoughlin (2 hours) vs Alcock (8 hours at mortuary)
Paul (2024): requirement of an accident satisfied here
Ordinary fortitude foreseeability
Conclusion for each
questions.modelAnswer:
Each claimant has a recognised psychiatric illness (Hinz v Berry 1970), so the issue is whether a duty is owed. None was personally in physical danger, so all are potentially secondary victims and must satisfy the Alcock v CC South Yorkshire (1992) controls. Since Paul v Royal Wolverhampton (2024), there must be an accident, an external event causing or threatening injury, which a stage collapse plainly is.

Cara: as Ben's wife she has a presumed close tie of love and affection. She was present at the scene and perceived the collapse with her own senses. Psychiatric injury to a person of ordinary fortitude seeing a spouse crushed is foreseeable. She is likely to succeed.

Dev: a brother's tie is not presumed and must be proved; in Alcock brothers failed for want of evidence. More fundamentally, he perceived the events on a live stream. Alcock held that watching on television did not satisfy proximity or perception with one's own unaided senses, especially as broadcasting codes prevented images of identifiable individuals suffering. A live stream raises similar problems, though one might argue that unfiltered footage of an identifiable relative differs. His claim is likely to fail.

Eli: a rescuer has no special status (White v CC South Yorkshire 1999). He was never in danger and did not reasonably believe he was, so he is not a primary victim under Page v Smith (1996). He has no relevant tie to Ben, so fails as a secondary victim.

Fay: as Ben's mother her close tie is presumed. The question is whether three hours later at the hospital is within the 'immediate aftermath'. In McLoughlin v O'Brian (1983) a mother who arrived at hospital about two hours after the accident and saw her family before they were cleaned recovered; in Alcock identifying a body at the mortuary eight hours later was too late. Fay's situation is closer to McLoughlin, so she has a reasonable prospect.

Conclusion: Cara and probably Fay succeed; Dev and Eli fail.

questions.q: Greenfields Holiday Park has a lake with a sign at the car park saying 'Swimming at your own risk'. Kai, a 9-year-old guest, wanders unsupervised to an unfenced jetty with rotten boards, falls through and is injured. Zara, 25, climbs the fence of the adjoining closed boatyard (also occupied by Greenfields) at night to swim from the slipway and is injured by submerged machinery the manager knew had been dumped there and that local youths often swam. An electrician, Ravi, hired by the park, is electrocuted by faulty wiring he was called in to repair. Advise the park.
markScheme: Greenfields is occupier (Wheat v Lacon)
Kai: visitor under OLA 1957; common duty of care s2(2)
Children: s2(3)(a), less careful; jetty rotten boards as danger (Glasgow v Taylor allurement)
Parental responsibility (Phipps) at 9 years less persuasive; warning sign inadequate under s2(4)(a) and not aimed at jetty
Exclusion of liability for negligence causing personal injury void (UCTA s2(1)/CRA s65)
Zara: trespasser under OLA 1984; s1(3) conditions: knowledge of danger and of presence; reasonable to protect
Tomlinson: obvious risk of swimming vs hidden submerged machinery is not obvious
Ravi: specialist under s2(3)(b), Roles v Nathan: risk incident to his calling
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Greenfields has control of the park and boatyard and is the occupier of both (Wheat v Lacon 1966).

Kai: as a guest he is a visitor, so the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 applies. Greenfields owes the common duty of care in s2(2). Under s2(3)(a) it must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults, and an accessible jetty over water may act as an allurement (Glasgow Corporation v Taylor 1922). Phipps v Rochester (1955) places primary responsibility for very young children on parents, but a 9-year-old wandering in a holiday park is foreseeable. The danger was not the lake but rotten boards, a defect in the premises. The car park sign does not address the jetty and could not enable a child to be reasonably safe (s2(4)(a)). As a business occupier Greenfields cannot rely on the notice to exclude liability for personal injury caused by negligence (UCTA 1977 s2(1); CRA 2015 s65). Liability is likely; a 9-year-old is unlikely to be found contributorily negligent.

Zara: she is a trespasser in the boatyard, so the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 governs. Under s1(3) a duty arises if Greenfields knew of the danger (the manager knew of the machinery), knew or had reasonable grounds to believe trespassers might come near it (youths often swam there), and the risk was one against which it might reasonably be expected to offer some protection. Tomlinson v Congleton (2003) denies a duty for obvious risks such as diving into shallow water, but hidden submerged machinery is not an obvious risk inherent in swimming. A duty probably exists, discharged by a warning or by removing the machinery (s1(5)). Damages may be reduced for contributory negligence in trespassing at night.

Ravi: he is a visitor, but under s2(3)(b) an occupier may expect a specialist to appreciate and guard against risks ordinarily incident to his calling (Roles v Nathan 1963). Faulty wiring he was called to repair is such a risk. Greenfields is unlikely to be liable.

Conclusion: liability to Kai, probable liability to Zara, none to Ravi.

questions.q: Mira owns a house next to the Rook Arms pub, which last year built a beer garden with outdoor music until midnight. Mira's lodger, Theo, cannot sleep. Mira also complains that oil stored in drums at the pub, unusual for a pub, leaked into her cellar, damaging stored furniture and making her ill from the fumes. The pub argues it had planning permission for the garden and that Mira moved in only six months ago. Advise Mira and Theo.
markScheme: Private nuisance: amenity interference by noise
Standing: Mira has proprietary interest; Theo, as lodger/licensee, cannot sue (Hunter)
Reasonableness: locality, duration, timing; Fearn: ordinary use of land and substantial interference
Planning permission not a defence (Coventry v Lawrence) but relevant to locality/remedy
Coming to the nuisance no defence (Sturges; Coventry)
Remedy: injunction prima facie; damages in lieu under Coventry flexible approach
Oil: possible Rylands: bringing onto land, exceptionally high risk, non-natural use (Transco), escape, foreseeable damage (Cambridge Water)
Rylands excludes personal injury (Transco; Hunter): illness claim must be in negligence
Property damage recoverable; alternative claims in nuisance/negligence
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Noise: interference with sleep by late-night music is a classic amenity nuisance. Only a person with a proprietary interest or exclusive possession may sue (Hunter v Canary Wharf 1997), so Mira, the owner, has standing, but Theo, a lodger with a licence, does not.

The question is whether the interference is unreasonable. In Fearn v Tate Gallery (2023) the Supreme Court asked whether the defendant's use was a common and ordinary use of land and, if not, whether it substantially interfered with the claimant's ordinary use. Running a pub may be ordinary, but amplified outdoor music until midnight next to houses arguably goes beyond it, and frequent late-night noise is a substantial interference. Locality matters for amenity claims (Sturges v Bridgman 1879). Planning permission is not a defence, though it may bear on the character of the locality (Coventry v Lawrence 2014). Coming to the nuisance is no defence (Sturges; Coventry), and anyway the garden predates Mira's arrival by only months. Mira may seek an injunction, perhaps limiting hours; after Coventry the court may instead award damages in lieu, considering public interest and planning status.

Oil: Mira may rely on Rylands v Fletcher (1868). The pub brought the oil onto its land; storing it in drums may pose an exceptionally high risk if it escapes and, being unusual for a pub, may be an extraordinary use (Transco v Stockport 2003). It escaped to her land and caused foreseeable damage of the relevant type (Cambridge Water 1994). Some doubt arises because storing oil is often treated as ordinary, but Mira can alternatively claim in nuisance or negligence for the property damage. Her illness cannot be recovered under Rylands or private nuisance, which protect interests in land, not personal injury (Transco; Hunter); she must sue in negligence, showing a breach in how the drums were maintained.

Conclusion: Mira likely obtains relief for the noise and recovers for the furniture; her illness requires a negligence claim. Theo has no claim in nuisance.

questions.q: The Daily Probe publishes online an article headed 'Councillor's cash for planning?', suggesting that Councillor Jo Patel took bribes. It quotes an anonymous source and says Jo 'did not respond', though she was emailed only an hour before publication. The article also reveals that Jo had been receiving treatment for alcoholism, with a photograph of her leaving a clinic. A reader comments that the article is 'proof Patel is a crook'. Advise Jo.
markScheme: Defamation: meaning (bribery) defamatory; reference; publication
Serious harm s1, Lachaux: gravity and scale of online publication support inference
Truth s2: must prove substantial truth of bribery imputation
Honest opinion s3 unlikely: factual allegation
Public interest s4: matter of public interest, but reasonable belief: inadequate time to respond, anonymous source (Serafin)
Commenter: separate publisher; website operator defence s5 for the Probe re comments
Misuse of private information: health information has reasonable expectation of privacy (Campbell)
Photograph of clinic visit adds intrusion (Campbell)
Balancing Art 8/10: limited public interest in health; politician status not sufficient
Remedies: damages, injunction; limitation one year
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Defamation: the headline and article, read as a whole by the ordinary reasonable reader, bear the meaning that Jo took bribes, or at least that there are reasonable grounds to suspect it. The question mark does not prevent a defamatory meaning. She is named, and publication was online. Under the Defamation Act 2013 s1 she must show serious harm. After Lachaux (2019) this is a question of fact, but harm can be inferred from the gravity of an accusation of corruption and the scale of online publication.

Defences: the Probe could plead truth (s2) but must prove the bribery imputation substantially true, which an anonymous source alone is unlikely to do. Honest opinion (s3) fails because the allegation is factual. The main defence is public interest (s4). Corruption by a councillor is plainly a matter of public interest, but the Probe must show it reasonably believed publication was in the public interest. Serafin v Malkiewicz (2020) shows the court considers all the circumstances, including the reliability of sources and whether the claimant was given a fair opportunity to respond. One hour's notice and reliance on an unverified anonymous source make the defence weak.

The reader's comment is a separate publication by the commenter. The Probe, as website operator, may rely on s5 if it did not post the statement and responds properly to a notice of complaint.

Misuse of private information: information about treatment for addiction is health information in which Jo has a reasonable expectation of privacy (Campbell v MGN 2004). The photograph of her leaving a clinic increases the intrusion, as in Campbell. At the balancing stage the court weighs Article 8 against Article 10. Her status as a councillor may justify some reporting relevant to her public role, but her medical treatment appears unconnected to the alleged bribery, and the photograph adds little public interest value. The Article 8 claim is likely to prevail.

Remedies: damages and an injunction against further publication of the health material; the defamation claim must be brought within one year.

Conclusion: strong claims in both torts.
