questions.q: Speedy Deliveries engages Nina through an app; she wears its uniform, must follow its routes and can be removed at any time, but is labelled 'self-employed'. While delivering a parcel she gets into an argument with the customer, Omar, and punches him. Earlier that day Nina drove negligently and injured Pete, a cyclist who was not wearing a helmet and had been drinking; the injury to his head would have been less severe with a helmet. Advise Omar and Pete against Speedy.
markScheme: Two-stage test: relationship akin to employment; close connection (Catholic Child Welfare; BXB)
Label not decisive; Cox factors: integral to business, benefit, risk created; control
Barclays: not independent business carrying on own account
Close connection: Mohamud: argument flowing from job vs Morrison 2020 personal vendetta
Omar likely succeeds if assault arises from delivery interaction
Pete: negligent driving in course of work: vicarious liability straightforward
Contributory negligence for no helmet: Froom analogy; reduction if injury worse due to failure
Drinking: relevant only if causally contributed to accident or injury
Apportionment under 1945 Act: blameworthiness and causal potency
Conclusion with estimated reductions
questions.modelAnswer:
Vicarious liability requires (1) a relationship of employment or one akin to employment and (2) a close connection between that relationship and the tort (Various Claimants v Catholic Child Welfare Society 2012; BXB 2023).

Stage one: the 'self-employed' label is not decisive. Under Cox v MoJ (2016) the court asks whether Nina's activities are integral to Speedy's business, carried on for its benefit, and whether assigning them created the risk. Deliveries are the core of Speedy's business, Nina wears its uniform, follows its routes and is subject to its control. Barclays v Various Claimants (2020) excludes only genuinely independent contractors carrying on their own businesses. Nina appears to be part of Speedy's operation, so the relationship is at least akin to employment.

Omar: the question is close connection. In Mohamud v Morrison (2016) a kiosk attendant who followed a customer and assaulted him was acting within the field of activities assigned to him, in an unbroken sequence from his job of dealing with customers. In Morrison v Various Claimants (2020) an employee pursuing a personal vendetta was not. An argument arising from the delivery, escalating into violence at the customer's door, is closer to Mohamud. Speedy is likely liable, though a court would look carefully at whether the dispute was personal.

Pete: negligent driving while making deliveries is plainly within the close connection test, so Speedy is vicariously liable, assuming Nina was negligent.

Contributory negligence: under the Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 s1, damages are reduced as the court thinks just and equitable. By analogy with Froom v Butcher (1976), failure to wear a helmet where injury would have been less severe may justify a reduction of around 15%, though courts treat helmet cases with care and require evidence that a helmet would have reduced the injury. Drinking is relevant only if it contributed to the accident or injury; if Pete cycled normally, it is irrelevant. The court considers blameworthiness and causal potency (Jackson v Murray 2015).

Conclusion: Speedy is liable to both; Pete's damages may be reduced modestly.

questions.q: 'Since Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire (2018), the law on duty of care is clearer, but at the cost of leaving vulnerable victims of public authority failures without a remedy.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explain Caparo and its misreading as a universal test
Robinson: established categories and incremental development; acts vs omissions
Clarity gains: predictable outcomes, less policy-based reasoning by courts
Omissions principle applied to public bodies: Michael, Poole v GN, HXA v Surrey, Tindall
Statutory powers do not create duties (Gorringe; Stovin v Wise)
Critique: harsh outcomes for vulnerable (children in Poole; Tindall victim)
Alternative remedies: HRA Arts 2, 3 and 8 (Osman positive duties; DSD; Rabone); ombudsmen
Counterargument: separation of powers, resource allocation, defensive practice concerns
Remaining uncertainty: assumption of responsibility, 'making things worse' line
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Robinson sought to correct the misreading of Caparo (1990) as a universal three-stage test that invited courts to weigh policy in every case. Lord Reed held that where established principles apply, as when a positive act causes physical injury, a duty exists; novel cases develop incrementally. The decision was reinforced by a strict distinction between causing harm and failing to prevent it.

The gain in clarity is real. Before Robinson, police and public authority cases were often analysed as though public bodies enjoyed policy immunities, as in readings of Hill (1989). Robinson made clear that public authorities are subject to the same principles as private persons: liable for positive acts causing harm, but not generally for failing to confer benefits. Michael (2015), Poole BC v GN (2019) and HXA v Surrey CC (2023) confirm that statutory powers or functions do not by themselves create a duty (Gorringe 2004).

The cost is that victims of serious failings by protective agencies often have no negligence claim. In Poole, children whom the council had housed next to an abusive neighbouring family could not sue for its failure to protect them; in Michael, a delayed police response to a 999 call was not actionable; in Tindall, police left a known hazard and a driver died. Critics argue the act/omission line is artificial where a body has specialist knowledge and a statutory role, and that assumption of responsibility is unpredictable.

However, victims are not always without remedy. The Human Rights Act 1998 provides claims for operational failures to protect life or prevent ill-treatment under Articles 2 and 3 (Osman v UK 1998; Rabone 2012; DSD v Commissioner of Police 2018). The Supreme Court in Michael expressly considered the HRA a reason not to expand negligence.

There are also good reasons for restraint: courts are poorly placed to judge resource allocation, and liability may divert funds from front-line services.

Overall, the proposition is broadly correct: the law is clearer, and some victims lose. But the gap is partly filled by the HRA, and it reflects a principled choice about the role of tort rather than an oversight.

questions.q: 'The rules on recovery for psychiatric injury by secondary victims are arbitrary and should be replaced by a simple test of reasonable foreseeability.' Critically evaluate this claim in light of Paul v Royal Wolverhampton NHS Trust (2024).
markScheme: Explain primary/secondary distinction (Page v Smith; White)
Alcock control mechanisms and their rationale (floodgates, fraud, proportionality)
Arbitrariness examples: siblings in Alcock; TV; time limits on aftermath
Paul: 'accident' requirement; medical negligence cases excluded; reasoning on analogy with existing law
Paul's rationale: limiting the class to those most closely and directly connected and keeping rules certain; a doctor's role does not extend to protecting relatives
Law Commission (1998) proposals: abolish proximity requirements but keep close tie
Arguments for foreseeability alone: coherence, fairness, medical understanding of psychiatric harm
Arguments against: indeterminate liability, insurance costs, burden on defendants, legislative role
Lord Burrows' dissent in Paul
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Secondary victims, who suffer psychiatric illness from witnessing injury to another, face special controls. Alcock (1992) requires a close tie of love and affection, proximity in time and space to the event or its immediate aftermath, perception with one's own senses and foreseeability of psychiatric harm in a person of ordinary fortitude. Primary victims need only show foreseeable physical injury (Page v Smith 1996), and rescuers have no special status (White 1999).

The charge of arbitrariness has force. In Alcock brothers failed to recover because their close ties were not proved, and those who saw identifiable relatives die on television failed on perception. The boundary of the 'immediate aftermath', two hours in McLoughlin but not eight hours in Alcock, is hard to justify on medical grounds. Lord Steyn in White admitted the law was 'a patchwork quilt of distinctions'.

Paul v Royal Wolverhampton (2024) added a requirement that the claimant witness an 'accident', an external event causing or threatening injury. Relatives who saw a loved one collapse and die from negligently undiagnosed heart disease could not recover. The majority (Lord Leggatt and Lady Rose) did not claim that perceiving an event directly makes illness more deserving of compensation; they justified the limits by the need to confine claims to those most closely and directly connected to the event and to keep the rules certain and comprehensible, and held that a doctor's responsibilities do not extend to protecting relatives from witnessing a patient's death. Lord Burrows, dissenting, called the distinction drawn for medical negligence unprincipled, treated the relevant event as the death of the primary victim, which each claimant had witnessed, and would have allowed the appeals.

A foreseeability-only test would be simpler and arguably fairer, reflecting modern understanding that psychiatric illness is as real as physical injury. The Law Commission (1998) recommended abolishing the proximity and perception requirements while keeping a close-tie requirement. However, foreseeability is a weak limit: it is foreseeable that many people may be traumatised by news of a death. Unlimited liability could burden defendants and insurers disproportionately, and the class of potential claimants would be indeterminate.

The better view is that some controls are necessary, but the current rules draw lines in the wrong places. A statutory scheme based on close relationships, without arbitrary proximity rules, would balance fairness and certainty. After Paul, reform is a matter for Parliament.

questions.q: 'The courts' approach to factual causation in Fairchild and its successors is a pragmatic response to scientific uncertainty that undermines the coherence of tort law.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explain the but for test and its role in corrective justice
McGhee and Fairchild: material increase in risk for mesothelioma
Justification: injustice of denying recovery due to evidential gap; deterrence
Limits: single agent rule, Wilsher; Sienkiewicz extension to single defendant
Barker v Corus proportionate liability and Compensation Act 2006 s3
Distinguish material contribution to harm (Bonnington; Williams v Bermuda)
Loss of chance in Gregg v Scott as contrasting rejection
Coherence critique: liability without proof of causation; difficulty in confining exception
Defences of the approach: narrow and principled exception
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The orthodox 'but for' test requires the claimant to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the defendant's breach caused the harm. It reflects corrective justice: a defendant should compensate only harm they have done. In Fairchild v Glenhaven (2002) the House of Lords made an exception for mesothelioma: where several employers negligently exposed a claimant to asbestos and medical science cannot identify which fibres triggered the disease, each is liable if it materially increased the risk. This built on McGhee v NCB (1973).

The pragmatic case is strong. Without the exception, a claimant exposed negligently by every employer would recover from none, simply because of a scientific gap. Lord Bingham thought that result unjust and contrary to the protective purpose of the duty. The exception also preserves deterrence in a field of serious occupational harm.

The coherence objection is that liability is imposed without proof that the defendant caused the harm. Barker v Corus (2006) tried to reconcile this by treating the damage as the risk itself and making liability proportionate. Parliament reversed this for mesothelioma in the Compensation Act 2006 s3, imposing joint and several liability. Sienkiewicz v Greif (2011) extended Fairchild to a single defendant whose exposure added to environmental risk, which several justices accepted with evident unease. The result is a special rule driven by sympathy and legislation rather than principle.

The courts have, however, confined the exception. Wilsher v Essex AHA (1988) refused it where several different agents might have caused harm, and Gregg v Scott (2005) refused recovery for loss of a chance in clinical negligence. Material contribution to harm (Bonnington 1956; Williams v Bermuda 2016) is a separate doctrine for cumulative causes and is consistent with orthodox principle.

Overall, Fairchild is a principled but narrow departure. It disturbs coherence because its boundaries rest on the scientific features of one disease. Yet tort has always balanced corrective justice against fairness, and a clearly confined exception is preferable to an unjust rule. The greater threat to coherence comes from any future expansion beyond the single-agent mesothelioma context.

questions.q: Which statute governs the duty an occupier owes to lawful visitors?
questions.why: The 1957 Act imposes the common duty of care to visitors; the 1984 Act covers non-visitors such as trespassers.

questions.q: Under the Defamation Act 2013, what must a claimant show in addition to a defamatory meaning, reference and publication?
questions.why: Section 1 requires that the statement caused or is likely to cause serious harm to reputation; falsity is presumed and truth is a defence for the defendant to prove.

questions.q: Ruth asks her bank manager, Liam, at a meeting whether Apex Builders, a bank customer, is creditworthy, explaining she is about to pay it a £40,000 deposit for an extension. Liam replies, without checking, 'They're sound as a pound', adding nothing else. Apex is in fact near insolvency and collapses with Ruth's deposit. Separately, Ruth's neighbour Sol buys a house relying on a valuation report commissioned by his mortgage lender from Value Surveyors, which negligently missed subsidence. The house is worth £60,000 less than reported. Advise Ruth and Sol.
markScheme: Losses are pure economic loss; generally irrecoverable (Spartan Steel; Murphy)
Hedley Byrne: voluntary assumption of responsibility and reasonable reliance
Ruth: Liam knew purpose, specific transaction, business context; no disclaimer (contrast Hedley Byrne)
Caparo: defendant knew statement would be communicated to claimant for a specific purpose and relied on
Vicarious liability of bank for Liam
Sol: no contract with surveyor; Smith v Eric S Bush: duty owed to purchaser of modest house who relies
Any disclaimer subject to reasonableness (UCTA s2(2); Smith v Bush)
Measure of damages: difference between price paid and true value; SAAMCO/Manchester Building Society scope of duty
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Both claimants have suffered pure economic loss, which is generally irrecoverable in negligence (Spartan Steel 1973; Murphy v Brentwood 1991). Each must rely on the assumption of responsibility exception from Hedley Byrne v Heller (1964).

Ruth: A duty arises where the defendant voluntarily assumes responsibility for a statement and the claimant reasonably relies on it. Caparo (1990) identifies relevant features: the adviser knew the advice would be communicated to the claimant, for a specific transaction, and that she was likely to rely on it without further inquiry. Liam was told exactly why Ruth was asking and the sum involved. He answered in a business setting and in his professional capacity, and added no disclaimer, unlike the bank in Hedley Byrne itself. It was reasonable for Ruth to rely on a bank manager's assessment of a customer's finances. A duty is likely, and answering without checking falls below the standard of a reasonably careful banker. The bank is vicariously liable for Liam's negligence in the course of employment. Ruth recovers the lost deposit, subject to any argument that she should have made further enquiries (contributory negligence).

Sol: He has no contract with Value Surveyors, which was retained by the lender. In Smith v Eric S Bush (1990) the House of Lords held that a valuer instructed by a lender owes a duty to the purchaser of a modest house where the valuer knows the buyer is likely to rely on the report without commissioning a separate survey. That reasoning applies to Sol. Any disclaimer would have to satisfy the reasonableness test under UCTA 1977 s2(2) (or the Consumer Rights Act 2015 s62 fairness test), which failed in Smith. Damages are the difference between the price paid and the house's true value, here £60,000, being loss within the scope of the duty to value accurately (SAAMCO 1997; Manchester Building Society v Grant Thornton 2021).

Conclusion: both are likely to succeed.
